title: Institutions Can't Think on Their Own
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: This article uses higher education's response to AI as a case study in institutional failure to think critically—the very capacity universities claim to cultivate. The author opens with sardonic observations about higher education's favorite crisis tool: a committee given sixty minutes every other Thursday to think radically about the future. The deeper irony is that institutions run by PhD-credentialed leaders—people who are supposed to be the living proof of what a university education produces—have responded to AI with ignorance, ineffective bans, or undifferentiated ChatGPT adoption, none of which resembles strategic thinking. The article traces higher education's AI response from 2023 ignorance to 2026 more policies but still no strategy, arguing that institutions claiming to teach critical thinking and adaptive problem-solving should have been leading the world's response to AI rather than lagging it. The essay ends with a direct challenge to the credibility of higher education's value proposition: when institutions blame students for using AI rather than rethinking what education offers, they undermine their own claim to prepare people for a changing world.
points: Higher education's preferred crisis tool—a committee meeting for roughly 120 minutes per month—reveals a contradiction between the institution's promise of critical thinking and adaptability and its actual practice of slow, bureaucratic, calendar-bound response.

Institutions run by PhD-credentialed leaders are supposed to be the living portfolio of what their system produces—making their inadequate response to AI a direct test of whether a university credential actually delivers what it promises.

Higher education's AI response moved from 2023 ignorance to 2024 bans and committees to 2025 landscape analyses to 2026 more policies with still no coherent value proposition—a timeline that should embarrass institutions selling $60,000-per-year critical thinking.

The most radical strategies higher education has produced—total AI bans on one end, ChatGPT for everyone on the other—are neither strategic nor the kind of response an institution claiming to teach uncertainty-handling should be producing.

Blaming students for using AI to complete assignments while being unable to articulate why the education is worth $60,000 per year is the deepest institutional contradiction—the institution undermines its own value proposition by the very act of blame.
quotes: My favorite thing higher education does is form a committee to think radically about the future—and then give it sixty minutes every other Thursday to do so.

higher education claims to be the guardian and purveyor of learning and 'critical thinking,' and so I find it passing strange that the institution itself so frequently fails to demonstrate either of those competencies—or much related to them.

At the highest levels of leadership, institutions tend to be staffed by people holding all the credentials the institution provides—PhDs in essentially every leadership position. Given the logic of the claims higher education makes, these people ought to be the most adaptive, the best problem solvers, and the deepest critical thinkers.

The most radical—and perhaps clearest—'strategies' we have seen so far amount to total AI and technology bans on the one hand, and ChatGPT for everyone on the other. Neither seems particularly strategic.

When higher education looks at students using AI to complete assignments and blames them . . . When higher education bans AI because it cannot figure out another way . . . When higher education, in the midst of all this, says to prospective students, 'Come! We are going to teach you everything you need to succeed in a changing world' . . . Remind me again why we should believe them?
Still waiting on strategy. Still waiting on the value proposition that makes $60,000 a year worth it. Still wondering whether higher education gets it.
